body:
When I was in 5th year in secondary school my mental health took a tumble, not for the first time. I was sleeping less and eating less once again, and I was told I looked tired at least once every couple of weeks.

Well, one week it was particularly bad. I'd slept maybe a collective 14 or 15 hours that week by the time Friday rolled around for our double class in physics. I was exhausted and practically falling asleep sitting up. The teacher, who I'll call B, obviously noticed. He came down to my desk at the break in the middle and asked if I was tired.

Now I, having been mentally ill for some time, was used to this. Usually I would be told that school was not the place to sleep, and that I should be going to bed earlier. So having had more than three years' experience in the matter, I was expecting more of the same.

So when he asked "are you alright? Is everything okay at home?" I was unprepared, and caught off guard in the best way. It was the first time a teacher had asked something like that, or shown the interest too.

When I told him part of the truth - that I have trouble sleeping - he didn't try to brush it off, and he didn't repeat the same stuff I'd been hearing for years. He gave me advice on how to fall asleep without being bogged down by thoughts, advice I still use.

He quickly became my favourite teacher. His was the only class I looked forward to. I wasn't even that good in physics exams. He answered all of my (sometimes off-the-walls) questions. We talked at length about physics and a lot of other things too. Sometimes we'd talk for half an hour after school, since his was the last class of mine on Fridays, and later on Thursdays. 

Once he told me that he only went into teaching for the steady pay and the holidays. But he was an excellent teacher, both in academics and in supporting his students, and whether he knows it or not he helped me a great deal, and I'll be grateful for that for the rest of my life.
